topics.title: The Nurse as Collaborator and the Care Team
topics.summary: Collaboration means the whole team, including the client and family, shares one goal and combines skills without duplicate work, while the nurse links each problem to the right expert.
objectives: You can define collaboration and tell interprofessional from interdisciplinary.
You can describe the five groups a nurse collaborates with.
You can match a client’s problem to the right team member.
You can decide what the RN keeps and what can go to an LPN or UAP.
You can name the benefits of team care and the community programs that use it.
topics.bigPicture:
No one person can safely care for a hospital client alone. After a knee replacement, a client needs the surgeon, the nurse, the physical therapist, the case manager, and the social worker. Most of all, the team needs the client’s own goals. Collaboration turns that group of experts into one shared plan.

When teams do not work together, clients get repeat tests, mixed messages, and missed problems. When teams work well, errors, complications, deaths, and hospital stays all go down. The nurse sits at the center because the nurse is with the client around the clock. The NCLEX will ask who should be involved, what you can hand off, and what you must keep.
recap: Collaboration = common goal + combined skills + no duplicate work, with the client as a partner.
QSEN Teamwork and Collaboration is one of six competencies, split into knowledge, skills, and attitudes.
The nurse collaborates with clients, peers, other professionals, nursing organizations, and legislators.
Match problem to expert: PT walking, OT daily tasks, SLP swallowing, RD disease diets, social worker money and coping.
The RN keeps assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients. Use the five rights to delegate tasks.
Team care lowers errors, deaths, hospital stays, and cost, and raises staff satisfaction.
Community models: long-term care, schools, ACT for serious mental illness, and PACE for older adults.

keyTerms.def: Two or more people working toward a common goal by combining skills, knowledge, and resources, without duplicate work (WHO, 2010).
People from different professions working together. In this course it also includes support staff, the client, and the family.
A term often used to show that paraprofessionals, such as UAP or technicians, are on the team too.
Students from two or more professions learning with, from, and about each other.
One of six QSEN competencies: working well in teams through open communication, mutual respect, and shared decisions.
What a role is legally allowed to do under state law, job description, and agency policy.
Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as nurse aides and patient care technicians. They do tasks the RN delegates.
Handing a specific task to a competent person. The RN still holds accountability for the outcome.
Giving clients or care to staff whose own scope already allows that care.
Usually a nurse or social worker who coordinates care and resources across settings.
The RD is credentialed and provides medical nutrition therapy, meaning disease-specific diets. A nutritionist may lack credentials and teaches general healthy eating only.
Trouble swallowing. Coughing or a wet voice with drinks is a warning sign. The speech-language pathologist evaluates it.
ACT (Assertive Community Treatment) serves people with serious mental illness in the community. PACE (Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly) helps older adults stay home.

sections.heading: What is collaboration?
sections.keyIdea: Collaboration means one shared goal, combined skills, and no duplicate work, with the client as a partner.
sections.body:
The WHO says collaboration is two or more people working toward a common goal. They combine their skills, knowledge, and resources. They also avoid doing the same work twice.

Collaboration is not just being nice, and it is not just following orders. If the nurse and the physical therapist each teach a different way to climb stairs, they did not collaborate. They only worked side by side.

Henderson called collaboration a partnership with clients and families. The client has an equal voice. Answers that decide for the client lose to answers that set goals with the client.

Collaboration happens at three levels, listed below. To do it well, nurses need accountability, authority in their practice area, and ongoing learning about roles and group work.
bullets: The nurse with the client.
Healthcare providers with the client.
Providers from different professions with each other.
sections.analogy: A good team is like a pit crew, not a relay race. In a relay, each runner goes alone. In a pit crew, everyone works on the same car at once, each with a clear job. The driver, the client, says where the car goes.

check.q: A PT and a nurse each teach a client a different way to get out of bed after hip surgery. What is missing?
check.a: A common goal with non-duplicated effort. They should agree on one method and both teach it.

sections.heading: What does the profession expect of you?
sections.keyIdea: QSEN, ANA, and NLN make teamwork a core nursing duty; the client is your main partner.
sections.body:
Three nursing groups set this standard. QSEN (Quality and Safety Education for Nurses) makes Teamwork and Collaboration one of six core competencies. The ANA practice standards include a collaboration standard, which the course cites as Standard 10. The NLN (National League for Nursing) asks schools to teach students from different professions together.

Box 37.1 splits the QSEN competency into knowledge (what you understand), skills (what you visibly do), and attitudes (what you value). Exam items usually describe a skill.

Box 37.2 lists five groups a nurse collaborates with. The client group is tested most. Good verbs are involve, encourage, agree on. Wrong-answer verbs are decide for, tell, insist.
bullets: Clients: encourage involvement and independence, treat them as equals, and set goals together.
Peers: share expertise and build trust and respect.
Other professionals: respect their expertise, listen to every view, and share care-plan decisions and research.
Nursing organizations: serve on committees and support political solutions.
Legislators: give expert opinion on health laws, such as testifying on a bill.

table.caption: Box 37.1 QSEN skills you can see on a shift
rows: Act with integrity, respect other views, keep learning
Work within scope, ask for help, clarify roles
Ask for input, start conflict resolution
Use structured handoffs; accept that care transitions are risky
Help design systems that support teamwork

check.q: A new nurse has never titrated a heparin drip and asks the charge nurse to review the protocol with her. Which QSEN skill is this?
check.a: Scope and roles: working within her scope and asking for help when needed.

sections.heading: Who on the team owns which problem?
sections.keyIdea: Turn the client’s problem into a body function, then pick the team member whose scope covers that function.
sections.body:
Many NCLEX items really ask, “Who owns this problem?” First, turn the problem into a function, such as swallowing, walking, dressing, or diet. Then pick the team member whose scope matches. Often the nurse assesses first, then refers.

Two traps: only the registered dietitian gives medical nutrition therapy, like a kidney or diabetic diet. And check your Nurse Practice Act and agency policy before carrying out a physician assistant’s order.

table.caption: Table 37.1 team members and their clues
rows: Care under RN or provider supervision
Delegated hygiene, feeding, walking, vital signs
Diagnoses and treats under a physician
Lab and imaging data; electronic records
Acupuncture, massage, herbs; teeth and mouth

check.q: A client with rheumatoid arthritis walks well with a cane but cannot button her blouse or open jars. Who should she see?
check.a: Occupational therapy, for adaptive devices and daily-task training. PT is for walking, which she already manages.

sections.heading: What can the RN hand off?
sections.keyIdea: Delegate tasks, never the nursing process: assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients stay with the RN.
sections.body:
The RN is accountable for assessment, nursing judgment, planning, teaching, and evaluation. These are never handed off.

The LPN/LVN gives care under RN or provider supervision, usually to stable clients with predictable outcomes. UAP do tasks the RN delegates, like hygiene, feeding, and walking.

Delegation hands a task to a competent person, but the RN still owns the outcome. Assignment gives care to staff whose own scope covers it.

Use the five rights of delegation (NCSBN/ANA), listed below. Give specific directions, then follow up. For example: “Walk Mr. Ruiz 50 feet with his walker at 1000 and 1400. Tell me right away if he is dizzy or his pulse is over 110.”
bullets: Right task: routine and allowed for this worker.
Right circumstance: the client is stable and predictable.
Right person: the worker is competent and allowed by policy.
Right directions: what, when, and what to report.
Right supervision: check the result and reassess the client yourself.
sections.example: A client 4 days after a below-knee amputation needs a scheduled dressing change: that fits the LPN. A new admission needing assessment stays with the RN.

check.q: Which client could a UAP take vital signs on: one 2 hours after cardiac catheterization with a new irregular pulse, or one with stable COPD?
check.a: The stable COPD client. The new irregular pulse is unstable and needs the RN.

sections.heading: What does good teamwork achieve?
sections.keyIdea: Good teamwork means fewer errors and deaths, more satisfied staff, and lower costs.
sections.body:
Interprofessional collaborative practice is a care model where many professions, the client, and the family work as one team. The course lists seven aims for it, shown below.

The table links collaboration to its benefits and related concepts. On the exam, find what is getting better or worse in the stem. Then match it to a row. If teamwork is working, you should see fewer repeat tests, better staff retention, and fewer complications.
bullets: Client-centered care where the client takes part
Continuity from prevention to rehabilitation
Better client and family satisfaction
High-quality, cost-effective, evidence-based care
Mutual respect and communication
Fixing system problems
Providers and clients who depend on each other

table.caption: Benefits and related concepts
rows: Active partner; fewer complications, errors, and deaths; shorter stays
Less hierarchy; more respect; higher satisfaction and retention
Less duplicate service; lower cost; better access
Raises nurses’ sense of autonomy; nurses teach others about nursing roles
Raises situational awareness (noticing what is happening) and teamwork
Lowers morbidity (illness) and mortality (death); nurses raise concerns at team meetings

check.q: After a hospital starts team rounds, readmissions and duplicate imaging fall. Which concept does this show?
check.a: Healthcare systems: less duplication and lower cost. Fewer deaths would show safety.

sections.heading: Team care outside the hospital
sections.keyIdea: Teams matter in long-term care, schools, ACT for mental illness, and PACE for older adults.
sections.body:
Teams work together in the community too, as the list below shows.

Clinical Example A: Mr. Hainsley wants to go home after a knee replacement, even with stairs. The nurse, RN case manager, PT, social worker, and surgical resident meet with him and his spouse. They respect his goal, set up home health and a PT home-safety check, and solve money and equipment problems.

Clinical Example B: Mr. Eliot has heart failure, kidney failure, high blood pressure, and an enlarged prostate. Daily rounds with the nurse, physician, dietitian, and case manager address fluid overload, urine retention, and anxiety. His diuretic is lowered once stable, the dietitian teaches low sodium, and home care is set up.
bullets: Skilled nursing, rehab, long-term care: nursing, medicine, therapies, social services, and mental health.
Schools: nurses, teachers, counselors, therapists, and physicians for children with disabilities or fragile health.
ACT: psychiatrists, social workers, pharmacists, APRNs, job counselors, and peer specialists for serious mental illness.
PACE: medical care, respite (caregiver relief), rides, and mental health care so older adults can stay home.

check.q: A 34-year-old with schizophrenia keeps stopping his medicine. An 82-year-old wants to stay home, but her caregiver needs relief. Which program fits each?
check.a: ACT for the 34-year-old; PACE for the 82-year-old.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike roles and ideas
sections.keyIdea: Wrong answers often swap two similar roles, so learn the clue that separates each pair.
sections.body: These pairs look alike on the exam. Use the clue column to tell them apart fast.

rows: Interdisciplinary signals UAP or techs are included
Techs or aides on the team
RD gives disease diets; nutritionist teaches healthy eating
PT = walking and strength; OT = daily tasks
SLP tests swallowing; RD adjusts nutrition after
Coordinates services vs. coping, money, protection
Task handed off vs. care within own scope
UAP task vs. LPN client load
Serious mental illness vs. older adults at home
Client helps decide vs. told a decision

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The best answer keeps the client safe, respects scope, and involves the client.
sections.body:
Expect the three patterns below. The best answer keeps the client safe, respects scope, and involves the client.

Sample question: A client 3 days after a stroke coughs each time he drinks water, and his voice sounds wet. His daughter asks for thin liquids because “he hates thickened drinks.” Which action should the nurse take first?

A. Ask the dietitian to calculate fluid needs.
B. Hold oral fluids and request a speech-language pathologist swallowing evaluation.
C. Teach the daughter to give small sips through a straw.
D. Ask the UAP to stay with the client during meals.
bullets: Referral: a problem and four disciplines. Pick the matching scope.
Delegation and assignment: which client or task can go to the LPN or UAP.
Collaboration behavior: which action shows collaboration, or which statement needs more teaching.
steps: Read the stem: coughing and a wet voice with water after a stroke signal aspiration, meaning fluid entering the lungs.
What is it really asking? The FIRST action, so airway safety beats preference.
Key cues: swallowing problems belong to the SLP.
Why the others are wrong: A does not stop aspiration. C is unsafe; straws can raise aspiration risk. D does not fix unsafe swallowing.
The answer is B. Protect the airway, then get the expert. If an option said “assess breathing,” that would come first.
Strategy: turn the problem into a function, match it to a discipline, and keep the client safe first.

sections.heading: Worked case: a client who refuses rehab
sections.keyIdea: Build one plan with the client at the center, balancing her wishes and her safety.
sections.body:
Mrs. Alvarez, 78, is ready to leave after hip fracture repair. She lives alone up one flight of stairs, uses a walker, and takes 11 medicines. She says, “I am not going to a nursing home. My cat needs me.”

The surgeon wrote “discharge to rehab.” Her son worries she will fall. A coworker says, “Just tell her the doctor decided.”
steps: Spot the cues: fall risk, many medicines, a strong wish, family worry, and a plan made without her.
Clarify her goal: home with help, short rehab, or home health? Her wishes are the starting point.
Bring in experts: PT for stairs, OT for bathing and kitchen safety, pharmacist for medicines, case manager for options, social worker for cost.
Ask for a team conference with her and, with her permission, her son.
Document the shared plan, who owns each action, and follow-up.
Evaluate: Can she climb stairs safely and state her medicine schedule? Revise if not.

check.q: Why is “Just tell her the doctor decided” wrong, even if rehab is safest?
check.a: It removes her from the team. The team may still recommend rehab, but she keeps the right to decide.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the RN delegates only tasks on the aide’s approved list, never nursing judgment.
sections.body: These state rules match national delegation rules. The NCLEX does not test statute numbers.
bullets: NCBON regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
Practice rules: 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN). The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
The RN delegates tasks, not the nursing process or judgment. The LPN works under supervision.
Nurse Aide I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: NCBON; the aide must also be on the NA I registry.
NA II tasks include some advanced ones, like sterile dressing changes and oxygen tasks.
A task must be on the aide’s list AND right for that client. NCBON offers delegation and scope decision trees.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. You always follow the practice act of the state where the client is located. Confirm rules and policy before following a PA’s order.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Where this content comes from, plus updates.
bullets: Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2553–2556 (definitions, QSEN/ANA/NLN, Boxes 37.1–37.2, Table 37.1, related concepts) and pp. 2558–2559 (collaborative practice, community settings, Clinical Examples A and B).
The source says “National League for Nurses.” The correct name is National League for Nursing.
ANA Standard 10 is the 2015 numbering. The 2021 edition lists collaboration as Standard 11.
RDs/RDNs make nutrition diagnoses, not medical diagnoses.
Five rights and the no-delegating-assessment rule are standard NCSBN/ANA principles added here.

mnemonics.name: 5 Rights of Delegation
mnemonics.text: Task, Circumstance, Person, Directions/Communication, Supervision/Evaluation: “The Careful Person Directs and Supervises.”

mnemonics.name: Who owns the function?
mnemonics.text: PT = Paths (walking, stairs); OT = Occupations (dressing, cooking, daily tasks); SLP = Swallow and Speech; RD = Recipes for disease (medical nutrition therapy); SW = Support and Safety net (money, coping, protection).

pearls: Answers that set goals with the client beat answers that inform the client of decisions.
Coughing or a wet voice with fluids: hold oral intake and involve the SLP.
Disease-specific diets go to the registered dietitian, not a nutritionist.
Delegate tasks, never the nursing process.
Check state rules and policy before following a physician assistant’s order.
redFlags: A care plan made without the client’s input, especially one the client rejected.
A UAP assigned to a client whose condition is changing.
Signs of aspiration while the client still gets thin liquids.
Different disciplines giving the client conflicting instructions: call a team conference.

checks.q: A client with new type 1 diabetes and celiac disease wants a meal plan. A nutritionist is free today; the RD, tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Refer to the registered dietitian for medical nutrition therapy. Reinforce general information until then.

checks.q: Which is better: “The team decided you will go to rehab” or “The team recommends rehab. What concerns you about that?”
checks.a: The second. It keeps the client as a partner. The first is top-down.

checks.q: A UAP says a client who had a stroke 2 days ago sounded “gurgly” after juice. The order is thin liquids. What should the nurse do first?
checks.a: Assess the client’s breathing and hold further oral intake. Then request a swallowing evaluation by the SLP.

checks.q: A client has a new oxygen saturation of 88% and new confusion. What can the UAP do for this client?
checks.a: Only supportive tasks the RN directs after the RN assesses, like staying with the client. The client is unstable, so the RN must assess, intervene, and evaluate.

checks.q: A heart failure client is reviewed in daily team rounds. What data show the plan works?
checks.a: Weight dropping, clearer lungs, better oxygen levels, the client naming low-sodium foods, and home care set up.

topics.title: IPEC Team Skills and TeamSTEPPS Communication Tools
topics.summary: IPEC names four team competencies, and TeamSTEPPS tools like SBAR, call-out, checkback, CUS, and I PASS THE BATON make safety messages clear and complete.
objectives: You can name the four IPEC competencies and spot each one.
You can turn status-based words into team-centered words.
You can organize an SBAR call and an I PASS THE BATON handoff.
You can choose call-out, checkback, CUS, or the Two-Challenge Rule.
You can escalate an ignored safety concern up the chain of command.
topics.bigPicture:
Poor communication between providers is a major cause of harm. Most serious errors do not happen because someone forgot a dose. They happen because the person who noticed a problem did not say it clearly or was not heard. A nurse who says “he looks kind of off” assessed well but communicated poorly.

IPEC describes four team competencies: respect, roles, communication, and teamwork. TeamSTEPPS, built by the Department of Defense and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), gives you scripts. Scripts make key facts come out in the same clear shape, even under stress. They also flatten the hierarchy. A new graduate who says “This is a safety issue” carries the same weight as a 20-year veteran.
recap: IPEC’s four competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
Respect and trust are built over time through follow-through and listening. They are never automatic.
Team-centered talk (“we,” “what do you think?”) invites speaking up. Status-based talk silences people.
SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Assess before calling and always end with a request.
Call-out = the whole team hears a critical value at once. Checkback = repeat back, and the sender confirms.
CUS plus the Two-Challenge Rule: say it at least twice, require acknowledgment, then go up the chain of command.
I PASS THE BATON structures handoffs, including safety concerns, ownership, and next steps.

keyTerms.def: Interprofessional Education Collaborative. It names four core competencies for teamwork: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
Respect means valuing every member, including the client and aides, as equals. Trust means confidence in another’s actions. Both are built over time.
Top-down, one-way, or intimidating talk (“Just do it”). It keeps others from speaking up.
Talk that uses “we,” invites input, listens, and shares your own view honestly.
An evidence-based teamwork system from the Department of Defense and AHRQ. It standardizes communication to reduce errors.
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request. A set order for sharing critical client information.
Passing responsibility for a client to another nurse or provider, such as at shift change. It is high-risk.
Saying a critical fact aloud to the whole team at once during an urgent event.
Closed-loop talk. The receiver repeats the message, and the sender confirms it is correct.
A speak-up script: “I am Concerned. I am Uncomfortable. This is a Safety issue.”
Every member may voice a safety concern at least twice. If still ignored, the member takes stronger action and goes up the chain of command.
The next level of authority, one step at a time: charge nurse, then supervisor, then medical leadership, per policy.
A handoff tool: Introduction, Patient, Assessment, Situation, Safety concerns, (THE), Background, Actions, Timing, Ownership, Next.
When the whole team understands the plan, roles, and client status the same way. Built through huddles and team rounds.

sections.heading: What are the four IPEC competencies?
sections.keyIdea: IPEC’s four competencies are values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
sections.body:
IPEC (2016) names four competencies. They build on each other. You cannot talk well with someone you do not respect. You cannot use someone’s skills if you do not know their role.

Mutual respect and trust are not automatic. Health care has not always valued other professions. Teams build trust on purpose by following through, thanking people for good catches, and admitting limits.

Roles and responsibilities mean knowing each member’s scope. That lets the nurse say, “This is a question for the pharmacist,” instead of guessing. Each member also keeps learning and explains their role to the client.

table.caption: The four IPEC competencies
rows: Respecting the client’s and team’s values; treating all as equals
Ignoring an aide’s report because “she’s just an aide”
Explaining each member’s role to the client; calling the pharmacist for drug questions
Changing ventilator settings that belong to RT
Team goals first; client and family join rounds; shared decisions

sections.example: A UAP says, “Mrs. Park didn’t want breakfast and seems sleepier than yesterday.” The nurse says, “Thank you. That’s an important change. I’ll go assess her now.” Later, the nurse tells the aide what she found. The aide learns that speaking up matters.

check.q: A nurse tells a client, “The respiratory therapist will manage your breathing treatments, and the pharmacist will review your home medicines.” Which competency is this?
check.a: Roles and responsibilities. The nurse explains each member’s role and uses each person’s skills.

sections.heading: Status-based vs. team-centered talk
sections.keyIdea: Team-centered talk uses “we” and invites input, so people speak up and errors get caught.
sections.body:
Physicians are usually trained to speak briefly. Nurses often tell the whole story. Neither is wrong, but the mismatch causes friction. A long story at 0300 may lose the listener before the request.

One study of pediatric ICU family meetings found physicians spoke about 90% of the time. The family’s voice can get crowded out.

The bigger danger is status-based talk. It is one-sided and says “do not question me,” so people stay quiet. Team-centered talk uses “we,” asks for input, and shares your view honestly.

table.caption: Rewrite status-based words
rows: “You need to get him up now.”
“We want him walking before lunch. What time works for you?”
“His pain is 8/10 and respirations are 12. What do you think about the dose?”
“Thanks for flagging that. Let’s check the protocol together.”
“Mr. X is worried about rehab. How can we address that?”

check.q: Rewrite: “You need to tell the family visiting hours are over.”
check.a: For example: “He seems exhausted. Could we talk with the family together about a visiting plan that lets him rest?”

sections.heading: How do you make an SBAR call?
sections.keyIdea: Assess first, give the facts in SBAR order, and always end with a clear request.
sections.body:
SBAR puts critical facts in a set order. The situation comes first, and the call ends with a clear request.

Before you call, assess the client yourself. Review recent vital signs, labs, medicines, allergies, and code status. Have the chart in front of you.

Students most often miss the Recommendation. A call with no request leaves the provider guessing.
steps: Situation: who you are, who the client is, and what is happening now. “This is Jen, RN on 4 West, about Mr. Lee in 412. His oxygen saturation dropped to 87% on 2 L.”
Background: key context. “He is day 2 after bowel surgery, has COPD, and got hydromorphone 1 mg IV 40 minutes ago.”
Assessment: your data and what you think. “Respirations 10 and shallow, hard to arouse. I am concerned about opioid-related breathing depression.”
Recommendation: what you need. “I’d like an order for naloxone and for you to see him now.”
Close the loop: read back any orders, then document the call, the response, and the time.

check.q: A nurse reports: “Mrs. Diaz, 68, with pneumonia, has a temperature of 39.4°C, HR 118, BP 92/54, and new confusion. I think she may be developing sepsis.” What is missing?
check.a: The Recommendation. For example, ask the provider to see her now and request blood cultures, lactate, and fluids per the sepsis protocol.

sections.heading: Call-out, checkback, and safe handoffs
sections.keyIdea: Call-out tells the whole team at once; checkback confirms one exact message; handoffs need a set structure.
sections.body:
In an emergency, everyone needs key facts at once. A call-out says a critical value aloud to the whole team (“Blood pressure?” “86 over 60!”). Then everyone can plan the next step.

A checkback closes the loop on one message. The receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms. Use it for every verbal or phone order, critical lab, and medicine instruction. Do not save it for when you are unsure.

A handoff is risky because responsibility changes hands. QSEN asks nurses to accept that transitions are risky. I PASS THE BATON gives handoffs a set order, so safety items are not skipped.

table.caption: I PASS THE BATON
rows: Introduction: you, your role, the client
Situation: current status and recent changes
Safety concerns: critical labs, allergies, falls, infection
A linking word, not a step
Actions: what was done or is needed
Next: what is expected to happen

check.q: In handoff, which belongs under Safety concerns: a latex allergy, high fall risk, or 15 years of hypertension?
check.a: The allergy and fall risk. Long-term hypertension is Background.

sections.heading: How do you speak up when ignored?
sections.keyIdea: Say the concern at least twice with CUS; if the client is still unsafe, go one level up the chain.
sections.body:
Noticing a problem is only half the job. The client is safe only if your concern changes what happens. CUS gives words the whole team knows as a stop signal.

The Two-Challenge Rule says you have the right and duty to voice a concern at least twice. The other person must acknowledge it. If the client is still at risk, take stronger action. Go up the chain of command per policy.

NCLEX loves the “provider brushed me off” stem. Silence, only documenting, or following an unsafe order are wrong. Going straight to the CEO or state board first is also wrong.
steps: First challenge: state the concern with data. “Dr. Shah, the potassium is 6.2, and this order adds potassium.”
If dismissed, use CUS: “I am concerned about high potassium. I am uncomfortable giving this. This is a safety issue.”
Second challenge: repeat it and ask for a response. The other person must acknowledge it.
Still unresolved? Do not carry out the unsafe action. Notify the charge nurse or supervisor per the chain of command.
Keep the client safe while you escalate. Monitor, hold the drug, and document the facts.
sections.example: A nurse says, “I’m concerned about his heart rate of 128,” and “I’m uncomfortable discharging him.” The provider says, “Noted. Discharge him.” The next words are: “This is a safety issue. I need you to evaluate him before he leaves.”

check.q: The consent says left knee, but the right knee is prepped. The nurse has said so twice. The surgeon says, “We don’t have time.” What now?
check.a: Stop the procedure by calling a time-out, a pause to verify the procedure. Escalate right away to the charge nurse or perioperative supervisor.

sections.heading: What blocks teamwork, and what fixes it?
sections.keyIdea: Hierarchy, role confusion, and separate training block teamwork; shared rounds, huddles, and joint training fix it.
sections.body:
In true teamwork, team goals come before personal goals. Clients and families are members. They voice concerns, ask questions, and help decide. The expert on a topic leads that part, then the team decides together. The pharmacist leads on a drug interaction, but the plan belongs to the team and client.

Physicians tend to rate nurse–physician teamwork better than nurses do. The table shows barriers and fixes. The list shows how to bring families in and how to tell a program is working.

table.caption: Barriers and fixes
rows: TeamSTEPPS, team-centered talk, and leaders who back a speak-up culture
Interdisciplinary rounds where each role is clear
Follow-through and shared mental models from huddles and briefings
Standard tools: SBAR, checkback, I PASS THE BATON

bullets: Invite families to bedside rounds and ask which goals matter most.
Pause during rounds to answer their questions.
Signs a program works: fewer handoff errors, more staff who feel safe to speak up, and steady read-back of orders.

check.q: At rounds, the pharmacist raises a possible interaction between a new antibiotic and warfarin. How should the decision be made?
check.a: The pharmacist gives expert input. Then the team, including the client, discusses it and decides together.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike tools
sections.keyIdea: Match the tool to the message: everyone now, one person exactly, or a concern still ignored.
sections.body: These tools sound alike. Use the clue column to tell them apart.

rows: Call-out goes to the whole team; checkback is a loop between two people
Checkback needs the sender to confirm
CUS is the wording; Two-Challenge is saying it twice, then escalating
SBAR vs. I PASS THE BATON
SBAR is short, for provider calls; BATON is a fuller handoff
Situation = what is happening; Assessment = what you think it is
Values = respect and trust; roles = knowing scope
Go one level up; skipping to leaders or regulators first is wrong
Next step = charge nurse or supervisor

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The best answer is specific, uses data, closes the loop, and escalates if the client is still unsafe.
sections.body:
Items ask which tool the nurse used, how to finish an SBAR, which handoff item needs follow-up first, and what to do when a concern is dismissed. Vague, silent, or bypassing choices lose.

Sample question: During a rapid response, the physician says, “Give amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes.” Which response by the nurse is best?

A. “Okay, I’ll get it right away.”
B. “Amiodarone 150 milligrams IV over 10 minutes?” and waits for confirmation.
C. Announces to the room, “Heart rate is 168!”
D. “I’ll write it down and have you sign it after the code.”
steps: Read the stem: a verbal drug order in a noisy emergency carries high error risk.
What is it really asking? The best reply to a verbal order.
Key cues: an exact drug, dose, route, and rate. That is what checkback is for.
Why the others are wrong: A does not verify. C is a call-out, not a reply. D puts paperwork before verifying.
The answer is B: repeat the exact order and wait for confirmation.
Strategy: whole team now = call-out. One person, exact = checkback. Still unsafe = CUS, twice, then chain of command.

sections.heading: Worked case: the concern nobody wanted
sections.keyIdea: When the data say danger and the provider says wait, use SBAR, CUS, and the chain of command.
sections.body:
At 0230, Mr. Owens, 64, is one day after colon surgery. His HR rose from 88 to 122. His BP fell from 132/80 to 98/58. Urine output was 15 mL/h for 2 hours. He says, “Something feels wrong.”

The on-call resident says, “He’s probably in pain. Give his PRN and call me in the morning.” A coworker shrugs: “That resident hates being called.”
steps: Spot the cues: rising HR, falling BP, low urine, and a sense of doom. Think bleeding or sepsis, not pain.
Prepare: reassess, check the dressing and drains, review the last hemoglobin, and organize SBAR.
Call with a clear request: “Please come see him now and order a CBC and lactate.”
If dismissed, use CUS: “I am concerned he is bleeding. I am uncomfortable waiting. This is a safety issue.”
Still unresolved? Tell the charge nurse and supervisor, who can reach the attending (senior) physician. Call rapid response if criteria are met.
Monitor him closely, keep IV access, and document times, data, and responses.

check.q: Your coworker says a rapid response will “make the resident look bad.” How do you answer using IPEC values?
check.a: Client safety is the team’s shared goal and comes before anyone’s reputation. Rapid response is a system tool built for exactly this.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, telling the provider does not end your duty; the chain of command is how you meet it.
sections.body: NC law makes the RN accountable for follow-through, not just for making the call.
bullets: Under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
Charting “provider notified” does not end your duty if the client is still unsafe.

NCBON reviews practice events with a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool. It sorts human error (a slip), at-risk behavior (a drift, like skipping read-back), and reckless behavior (ignoring a serious risk).
In the general Just Culture model: console the nurse and fix the system after human error, coach at-risk behavior, and discipline reckless behavior.
Conduct issues like drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary violations, and privacy breaches are reported to the Board, not just the employer.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Where this content comes from, plus updates.
bullets: Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2556–2558 (IPEC, respect and trust, communication styles, TeamSTEPPS tools, I PASS THE BATON, teamwork, barriers).
IPEC updated its competencies in 2023 (Version 3). The same four domains remain.
TeamSTEPPS 3.0 (AHRQ, 2023) keeps all the tools taught here.
TeamSTEPPS calls the BATON “Safety” step “Safety concerns.” “THE” is a linking word, not a step.
Chain-of-command steps and rapid response were added as expected next steps.
The 89.9% physician speaking time comes from one pediatric ICU study. It shows a trend, not a rule.

mnemonics.name: CUS
mnemonics.text: Concerned → Uncomfortable → Safety issue: three rising steps that tell the team to stop and listen.

mnemonics.name: Match the tool to the message
mnemonics.text: Everyone needs it now = Call-out. One person needs it exact = Checkback. Still unsafe = CUS, twice, chain of command. Changing hands = SBAR or I PASS THE BATON.

pearls: Assess before you call. End every SBAR with a specific request.
Checkback is complete only when the sender confirms.
Use checkback for all verbal orders and critical values.
After two unanswered challenges, escalate. Never proceed or stay silent.
In handoff, give safety concerns and name who owns each pending task.
redFlags: A verbal order carried out without repeat-back and confirmation.
A safety concern dismissed while the client is getting worse.
A handoff that skips pending critical labs, allergies, or isolation.

checks.q: During a code, the nurse says loudly, “Potassium is 7.1!” Which technique is this?
checks.a: A call-out. It tells the whole team at once so everyone can plan the next step.

checks.q: A provider phones in “Furosemide 40 mg IV now.” The nurse repeats it and hangs up. What is missing?
checks.a: The sender’s confirmation. Checkback is not closed until the provider says it is correct.

checks.q: Which SBAR part is “I think he is fluid-overloaded”?
checks.a: Assessment, the nurse’s reading of the data.

checks.q: During handoff you learn a potassium of 2.9 from 2 hours ago was never reported. What do you do?
checks.a: It is a safety concern with no owner. Assess the client and notify the provider promptly.

checks.q: A manager wants nurses and physicians to share one picture of each client’s plan. What works best?
checks.a: Interdisciplinary bedside rounds with client and family, or daily huddles, backed by leaders.

topics.title: Conflict, Conflict Styles, and Workplace Incivility
topics.summary: Conflict is normal in health care; the nurse spots its type early, prevents what can be prevented, picks the right style, and never tolerates bullying that endangers clients.
objectives: You can classify conflict as intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, or interorganizational.
You can tell overt from covert conflict by behavior.
You can name common causes of conflict and ways to prevent it.
You can pick the best Thomas–Kilmann style for a situation.
You can manage conflict with staff, clients, and families step by step.
You can recognize incivility, horizontal violence, and bullying, and know how to respond.
topics.bigPicture:
Put many people with different training and goals on a busy shift, and disagreement is certain. Conflict can never be fully removed. A unit where “nobody disagrees” often has hidden conflict, like gossip and sick calls. The goal is to bring conflict out early and handle it well.

Why does this matter for clients? Unmanaged conflict blocks communication, and blocked communication harms clients. A new nurse who is mocked for asking questions stops asking. A family that feels ignored starts shouting, and the nurse avoids the room. When safety is at stake, the nurse stands firm.
recap: Conflict blocks problem solving and communication. It is normal and manageable, never fully removed.
Four levels: intrapersonal (inside one person), interpersonal (between people), intergroup (between groups), interorganizational (between organizations).
Overt conflict is open and easier to fix. Covert conflict hides in gossip, sarcasm, absenteeism, and lateness.
Prevent conflict: address issues early, privately, and calmly. Leaders share work fairly and define roles clearly.
Compete for safety, collaborate on complex issues, compromise under time pressure, avoid briefly to cool down, accommodate when you care less.
Never compromise or accommodate on client safety.
First move for conflict in progress: go somewhere private, stay calm, let each person speak, and focus on the client.
Incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, and bullying harm safety. Document and report them.

keyTerms.def: Disagreement among people, groups, or organizations that blocks problem solving and communication. Normal and manageable.
Tension inside one person from clashing expectations or roles, like choosing between a day job and family needs.
Conflict between two or more people over goals, personalities, territory, or control.
Conflict between teams or groups, often over resources or scope, like physicians vs. nurse practitioners over regulation.
Competition between organizations in the same market, like two hospitals or two nursing schools.
Overt conflict is open and visible. Covert conflict is hidden and shows up as gossip, complaining, passive-aggression, absenteeism, or lateness.
The skill of handling conflict differently depending on the situation. It grows with practice and self-awareness.
Five conflict styles based on assertiveness and cooperativeness: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating.
Assertiveness is how much you push for your own concerns. Cooperativeness is how much you try to meet the other person’s.
Harsh words, threats, or broad blame. It makes conflict worse. Use specific, private, respectful feedback instead.
Rude or disrespectful words or behavior, like eye-rolling, sarcasm, or public criticism.
Words or tone that humiliate, degrade, or intimidate a person.
Hostile behavior by a nurse or group of nurses toward a peer of equal standing.
Repeated, health-harming mistreatment, such as verbal abuse, intimidation, or sabotage like withholding report information.
Team training from aviation. Like TeamSTEPPS, it supports blame-free problem solving and speaking up.

sections.heading: What is conflict, and what are its levels?
sections.keyIdea: Conflict is normal; naming its level tells you who must be involved in solving it.
sections.body:
Conflict can arise between nurses and clients, among team members, within a unit, or across a whole organization. It blocks problem solving and communication, which threatens safety. Handled well, though, it drives growth. A nurse and a PT who disagree about early walking may build a better plan together.

Naming the level tells you who must help solve it. Intrapersonal conflict needs self-reflection and support. Interpersonal conflict is solved by the people involved, with help if needed. Intergroup conflict needs leaders and system fixes. Interorganizational conflict is handled at the leadership and policy level.

table.caption: Four levels of conflict
rows: A nurse is torn between a day shift that clashes with child care and exhausting nights
Two nurses clash over a new admission, and one belittles the other
ED and ICU staff disagree about who owns boarding clients
Two hospitals in one city compete with ads

sections.analogy: Conflict is like a smoke alarm. The goal is not to rip it off the wall. It is to respond early and find the source. Covert conflict is an alarm with the battery pulled: quiet, but the smoke is still there.

check.q: Pharmacy and nursing disagree over who checks infusion pump drug libraries. Which level is this?
check.a: Intergroup: two groups in opposition over responsibility.

sections.heading: Overt vs. covert conflict
sections.keyIdea: Overt conflict is out in the open; covert conflict hides in gossip, sarcasm, absences, and lateness.
sections.body:
Overt conflict is open. Two people disagree in a meeting, or a family says, “I am unhappy with my mother’s care.” Because everyone can see it, it is easier to fix.

Covert conflict hides. It shows up as complaining, gossip, and passive-aggressive comments. It also shows up as absenteeism and lateness. People see it differently, so it causes more stress and confusion.

A manager who sees more sick calls and break-room whispers after a schedule change should spot covert conflict. The fix is to bring it into the open in a safe, nonpunitive way.

rows: Spot the pattern; surface it safely

check.q: After a new charting system starts, several nurses arrive late and joke about “management’s brilliant idea.” No one has complained. What type of conflict is this?
check.a: Covert conflict, shown through lateness and passive-aggressive comments.

sections.heading: What causes conflict, and how to prevent it
sections.keyIdea: Find the source, then fix it at the right level, and address early cues before they grow.
sections.body:
Kim et al. (2017) group causes into individual, interpersonal, and organizational layers. The source points to the fix. A style mismatch needs self-awareness. Unclear roles need leaders to define who does what.

Watch for early cues: tension, arguments, a coworker being left out, acting out, and snide remarks. Address issues as they come up. Avoid destructive criticism. Stay calm, move the talk to a private place away from clients, and listen to the other view.

Leaders prevent conflict by sharing work fairly and defining roles. They invite concerns without punishment and recognize team wins and life events.

table.caption: Sources of conflict
rows: Personality, communication style, usual conflict habits
Incivility, low support, poor communication, education or generation gaps
Unclear roles, scope issues, workflow, work environment, scarce resources
Low confidence in the nurse, saving face after mistakes, old top-down habits
Lack of knowledge, poor coping, fear shown as anger, unmet needs
Disputes that, left alone, grow into bullying

bullets: Self-care lowers stress: know your triggers.
Try meditation, guided imagery, progressive relaxation, mindfulness, and self-compassion.
These lower stress, raise compassion, and improve client care.

check.q: Two nurses argue every week about restocking the code cart because no one was ever assigned the job. What is the source and the fix?
check.a: Organizational: an unclear role. Leaders should assign who owns the task, not just coach the two nurses.

sections.heading: Which conflict style fits the situation?
sections.keyIdea: No style is always right; choose by stakes, time, and investment, and never give ground on safety.
sections.body:
Thomas and Kilmann describe five styles on two scales. Assertiveness is how hard you push for your own concerns. Cooperativeness is how much you try to meet the other person’s.

Conflict competence means choosing the style the situation needs. Most people have a default style. Knowing yours helps you respond on purpose instead of by habit.

Temporary avoidance can help when emotions run high. Stepping away lets people calm down first. Sustained avoidance makes the problem fester.

table.caption: Thomas–Kilmann styles
rows: Overuse seems selfish and hurts relationships
Refusing a dose 10 times the usual
Complex issues where outcome and relationship both matter
Nurse and PT plan walks around pain-medicine timing
Both only partly satisfied; never on safety
Two nurses split a holiday shift
Trivial issue, need more facts, or hot emotions
Talking after the code, once calm
You care much less than the other person
Swapping breaks so a coworker can take a call about her child

check.q: A provider wants a sedative given to a client whose respirations are 8/min and offers “half the dose.” Which style should the nurse use?
check.a: Competing. Hold the drug and seek more evaluation. Half a dose is a compromise on safety.

sections.heading: How do you manage conflict in progress?
sections.keyIdea: Go private, cool things down, let each person speak, use facts, and solve with “we” around the client.
sections.body:
Be honest and respectful. State the issue with facts, not personalities. Let each person speak without interruption, and listen without judging. Focus on solutions, not blame, with safe client care at the center.

Use “we” language: “How can we fix the admission delay?” Avoid “you” commands like “You need to take the next admission.”

Organizations help by using TeamSTEPPS and Crew Resource Management. Individuals can use self-inventories, such as the Thomas–Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument or an emotional intelligence inventory.

Sick clients and families are often scared and feel a loss of control. Anger is often fear in disguise. Giving back some control calms things down.
steps: Ensure safety and privacy. Move away from clients; call security per policy if anyone may be harmed.
Calm things down. Stay calm and respectful; step away briefly only to let emotions settle.
Let each person speak without interruption. Summarize what you heard.
State the issue with facts, not personalities.
Use “we” to find solutions, with client care at the center.
Agree on who does what and when you will check back. Escalate to leaders if unresolved.
sections.example: A daughter shouts that her father’s call light was ignored. The nurse says, “You’re worried about your dad. Let’s step into the family room.” The nurse listens, admits the delay, and checks the client. Then she asks, “What would help him feel safer tonight? We could do hourly rounds.” The family regains some control.

check.q: After a charge nurse helps two nurses settle a dispute, which statement shows collaboration worked: “We each gave up something” or “We built a plan we both support and will check it Friday”?
check.a: The second. Collaboration fully meets both people’s needs. “Each gave up something” is compromise.

sections.heading: What are incivility and bullying?
sections.keyIdea: Incivility, verbal abuse, horizontal violence, and bullying harm communication and safety, so report them, never normalize them.
sections.body:
Outcome 37.6 asks you to describe these behaviors and their effects. Incivility is rude behavior, like eye-rolling, sarcasm, or public criticism. Verbal abuse attacks dignity through words or tone. Horizontal violence is hostility between peers, the old “nurses eat their young.” Bullying is repeated, health-harming mistreatment, including sabotage like withholding report details.

Targets stop asking questions, delay calling for help, and leave nursing. Do not join in. Address it early when safe, document specifics, and report through the chain of command and policy. Leaders must enforce a zero-tolerance code of conduct.

rows: Eye-rolling when a new nurse asks a question
Yelling “Are you stupid?” at the station
Senior nurses exclude and undermine a peer
Repeatedly withholding key report details from one nurse
Private, specific feedback about a missed assessment

check.q: One nurse keeps giving a coworker the heaviest load and leaving details out of her handoffs. Another snapped once during a code and apologized. Which is bullying?
check.a: The first. Bullying is repeated and can include sabotage. A single snap with an apology is incivility, but not a pattern.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alike styles and terms
sections.keyIdea: Ask who wins, how long it lasts, and whether the target is the issue or the person.
sections.body: These pairs are easy to mix up. Use the clue column.

rows: Win–win that fully meets both vs. each gives something up
Sidesteps the issue vs. gives in to the other
Firm stand on an issue, often safety, vs. repeated attacks on a person
Groups or professions vs. separate organizations
Inside one person vs. between people
One nurse’s dilemma vs. two nurses clashing
Cools emotions vs. lets conflict fester
Rude and public vs. specific, private, and respectful

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: For conflict in progress, secure privacy and calm first, then listen to everyone, then solve.
sections.body:
Items ask which style fits, which conflict type is shown, what the charge nurse does first, and how to answer an angry family. Watch the setting, the stakes, time pressure, and each side’s power.

Sample question: Two staff nurses argue loudly at the nurses’ station about who will take a new admission. Clients and visitors can hear. Which action should the charge nurse take first?

A. Assign the admission to the nurse with the lighter load.
B. Ask both nurses to step into the conference room to discuss it.
C. Tell both nurses the argument will be reported to the manager.
D. Ignore the argument and let the nurses resolve it.
steps: Read the stem: a loud, public, interpersonal conflict near clients.
What is it really asking? The FIRST action.
Key cues: “loudly” and “clients and visitors can hear.” The first problem is the location.
Why the others are wrong: A skips hearing both sides and leaves the public scene. C is a threat that escalates. D is sustained avoidance and exposes clients.
The answer is B: move the talk to a private place, then hear each side and solve the assignment.
Strategy: secure safety and privacy, then listen, then solve. Threats, public decisions, and ignoring are distractors.

sections.heading: Worked case: a preceptor and a near miss
sections.keyIdea: Repeated mistreatment that affects client safety needs leaders and a safety report, not just “work it out.”
sections.body:
Kayla, a new graduate in week 6 of orientation, talks to the charge nurse. Her preceptor rolls her eyes at questions and called her “useless” in front of a client. Yesterday the preceptor left a fluid restriction out of report. Kayla gave the client a large pitcher of water, and another nurse caught it.

Kayla is thinking of quitting and asks the charge nurse not to “make it a big deal.” The preceptor is well liked and has worked there 15 years.
steps: Spot the cues: eye-rolling and public put-downs (incivility, verbal abuse), withheld report (sabotage), a pattern (bullying), and a near miss.
Analyze: interpersonal conflict that has become bullying. The power gap makes it hard for Kayla to fix alone.
Prioritize: client safety and Kayla’s safe practice come before keeping it quiet. Validate her and explain why it must be addressed.
Act: document specific incidents, report the near miss through the safety system, notify the manager, and assign a temporary new preceptor.
The manager meets privately with the preceptor, states the facts, and sets expectations. A guided talk may follow if Kayla agrees.
Evaluate: Kayla feels safe to ask questions, handoffs are complete, and no new incidents occur.

check.q: Why isn’t “Talk to her yourself and try to get along” the best response here?
check.a: The behavior is repeated, involves a power gap, and already affected client safety. Leaders and a safety report are needed.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: NC uses Just Culture for honest errors, but conduct issues like impairment go to the Board.
sections.body: NC rules support blame-free problem solving while still protecting the public.
bullets: NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool. It separates human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior.
This fits the course message: use blame-free problem solving (TeamSTEPPS, CRM) and let staff speak up without fear.
A near miss from an incomplete handoff is reported and used to fix the system, not hidden.
Conduct issues go to the NCBON, not just the employer: drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and privacy breaches.
NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders.
If a colleague seems impaired on duty, remove them from client care per policy, tell the supervisor, and report properly.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Where this content comes from, plus updates.
bullets: Source: Module 37 study guide, pp. 2559–2562 (conflict, levels, overt and covert, causes, prevention, Table 37.2 styles, management, clients and families, conflict competence) and p. 2563 (incivility terms; Outcome 37.6).
The source says compromising addresses the issue “though at the very least.” In Thomas–Kilmann terms it is medium on both scales: more direct than avoiding, less deep than collaborating.
Assertive and cooperative ratings for each style were added from the Thomas–Kilmann model.
Collaborating takes time and is not for emergencies, where a clear directive approach is needed.
Response steps for incivility reflect current guidance, such as ANA’s position on incivility, bullying, and workplace violence.

mnemonics.name: Who wins? (Thomas–Kilmann)
mnemonics.text: Competing = Me. Accommodating = You. Avoiding = Nobody (for now). Compromising = Half each. Collaborating = Both, fully.

mnemonics.name: PAUSE for conflict in progress
mnemonics.text: Private place, Allow each to speak, Use facts not feelings, Solutions with “we,” Evaluate and follow up.

pearls: Move heated talks to a private place before trying to solve them.
Compete to protect safety. Never compromise or accommodate on safety.
Brief avoidance to cool down is fine. Long-term avoidance makes conflict worse.
Gossip, sarcasm, sick calls, and lateness signal covert conflict.
Angry families are often scared. Involve them in decisions to restore control.
redFlags: Report details withheld as part of a personal conflict.
Arguments or put-downs in front of clients and families.
A family member making threats: ensure safety and call security per policy.

checks.q: Gossip and sick calls rise after a new self-scheduling policy. What type of conflict is this, and what is the first step?
checks.a: Covert conflict. Bring it into the open in a safe, nonpunitive forum that invites honest feedback.

checks.q: A coworker asks to swap weekend shifts. The nurse has no plans and does not mind. Which style fits?
checks.a: Accommodating. The nurse cares much less about the outcome than the coworker.

checks.q: A nurse and an RT start arguing during a code about who documents. What should happen?
checks.a: Put off the debate, not the documentation. The code leader assigns a recorder now. They settle the role question later, when calm.

checks.q: A nurse says to a new graduate in front of a client, “Didn’t they teach you anything?” What should a witness do?
checks.a: Recognize incivility. Do not join in, support the new nurse, and address it privately or report it per policy.

checks.q: Staff complain that “the same people always get the hardest assignments.” What prevents more conflict?
checks.a: Set clear, fair criteria for sharing the workload and invite staff feedback on them.
